description: Width tiers and ACARA elaborations for Music Years 7-8. Flat lookup by code — C, D, E and P strand standards. Renderer merges with node map files at runtime via code key.
subject: Music

width_notes.minimum_width: Anchored to the primary command term of the descriptor — the defensible floor. For all Music strands: the narrowest single context or task type that honestly satisfies the command term. For C/P: minimum is one composition or performance with identifiable technique application. For D: minimum is one practice context with documented outcomes. For E: minimum is one style or cultural context investigated.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in most common elaboration cases — sound standard practice. For C: range of compositional purposes, styles and documentation formats from elaborations. For D: range of practice types and tools. For E: range of styles, cultural contexts and investigative purposes. For P: range of performance contexts and audiences.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions — additional task contexts, genres, cultural settings or purposes. Must add context rather than difficulty. First Nations Australian music contexts included where elaborations indicate them. Example directions only — not exhaustive or prescriptive.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA v9 elaborations verbatim. Source data for the width tiers.

AC9AMU8C01.minimum_width: Interpret a piece of music in one style, applying at least two vocal/instrumental techniques that realise a specific stylistic feature; use a notation or documentation format (score, chart, recording or tablature) as a basis for the interpretation.
AC9AMU8C01.typical_width: Interpret music across a range of forms and/or styles; trial and select techniques that manipulate dynamics, timbre, articulation and accent/stress to realise stylistic features; use student and teacher goals to focus rehearsal; work from a range of notation formats including staff notation, tablature, graphic scores and recordings.
wider: Experiment with effects such as distortion, decay or delay in digital or amplified performance contexts to achieve stylistic feel; evaluate how these change the expressive character of the music
Use a recording and a chart (melody, form and harmony/chords) to develop an arrangement of a song, making deliberate interpretive decisions about elements the chart leaves unspecified
Investigate how accent and stress placement changes the feel of a melodic or rhythmic pattern — connect observations to genre-specific performance conventions such as swing feel or syncopation
elaborations: investigating and trialling ways of realising stylistic features when rehearsing; for example, using effects such as distortion, decay or delay, or using accent/stress to achieve a stylistic feel when interpreting melodies or rhythmic patterns

interpreting music that is notated/documented in a range of formats, such as graphic or interactive scores, staff notation or tablature (TAB) and recordings; for example, using a recording and a chart that includes melody, form and harmony/chords to develop an arrangement of a song
using student and teacher set goals as a focus for practising and rehearsing a range of solo and/or ensemble music

manipulating sound quality by applying understanding of the range of sounds/timbres that different instruments and voice types can produce; for example, manipulating dynamics and timbre in voice or acoustic or digital instruments to create a specific effect

AC9AMU8C02.minimum_width: Compose music using at least one element of music and one compositional device to communicate an identified idea, perspective or meaning; document the composition in at least one format appropriate to the style.
AC9AMU8C02.typical_width: Compose music for different purposes (ensemble repertoire, theatrical/media work, personal expression) using elements of music and compositional devices including patterns such as harmonic, rhythmic or melodic ostinati; notate, document or record using software or other formats appropriate to the genre and intended performers.
wider: Write a song or instrumental piece communicating a perspective on a local or social issue (sustainable living, relationships, identity); evaluate whether the musical choices support the message
Develop an arrangement or re-imagining of an existing melody, riff or chord progression, documenting the interpretive choices made in a format appropriate for the musicians performing it
Create a composition built from loops or layered ostinati, then compose or improvise additional melodic lines; evaluate how the layers interact and what the looped structure makes possible
elaborations: writing songs or instrumental music to communicate ideas or opinions about themes or issues, such as their perspectives on local issues relating to sustainable ways of living or relationships such as friendship
combining and manipulating the elements of music in ways that are characteristic of selected styles, creating and notating, documenting and/or recording a composition, using available digital tools

using patterns such as harmonic, rhythmic or melodic patterns as the basis for improvisation or composition; for example, creating a composition entirely from loops or recording a series of loops (ostinati/repeating patterns) and then composing/improvising additional melodic lines

composing music for different purposes, such as repertoire for an ensemble to perform or music for a theatrical, site-specific or media work; for example, a fanfare or other composition that will grab the audience's attention at the start of an event, ritual or ceremony
using software to notate, document and/or record compositions in formats that are appropriate to a genre, style or instrument, such as chord charts or percussion notation

arranging a familiar music piece into a different music style by manipulating the elements of music to convey meaning, and documenting the arrangement in a form that is appropriate, considering the style and the preferences of the musicians who might be performing the arrangement; for example, arranging an instrumental work for choral performance
developing an arrangement or re-imagining of an existing melody/tune by improvising, using given material such as a melody, riff or chord progression

AC9AMU8D01.minimum_width: Practise at least one listening/aural skill and one vocal/instrumental technique with a focus on manipulating an element of music to achieve an intended expressive effect; document the outcome in at least one format.
AC9AMU8D01.typical_width: Develop listening/aural skills and technical/expressive performance skills (intonation, phrasing, dynamics, articulation) across a range of practice contexts; extend and vary harmonic, rhythmic or melodic patterns; experiment with digital tools for arranging or creating effects; document ideas, decisions and progress using a journal, notation, charts or recordings.
wider: Record alternative approaches to interpreting a phrase or melody and evaluate each against the intended expressive effect — use the recording to identify what the ear notices that playing alone doesn't reveal

Identify chord qualities in isolation, experiment with different orderings to create a chord progression, then improvise a melody over the progression; evaluate how the progression shapes the melodic possibilities
Use digital tools to write additional parts (e.g. a bassline to accompany a melody) and evaluate how added parts change the musical texture and expressive character
elaborations: experimenting with ways in which vocal/instrumental techniques can be used to manipulate elements of music to achieve intended effects, such as an expressive sound that is typical of a particular style, and transcribing or documenting their ideas as a reference for future performances or composition
practising technical and expressive skills such as intonation, pitch/rhythmic accuracy, phrasing or shaping dynamics and articulation to communicate expressive intent using voices and/or instruments

developing techniques for extending/varying patterns such as harmonic, rhythmic or melodic patterns; for example, identifying qualities of chords in isolation and experimenting with different ways to order the chords to create a chord progression and improvising over the progression, or using the chord progression in a song or instrumental music

experimenting with ways in which digital tools can be used when arranging musical ideas or creating effects; for example, using digitally produced parts alone or in combination with voice/vocalisation or other instruments

developing ability to manipulate and control elements of music to enhance performance and communicate intentions; for example, recording alternative approaches to interpreting a phrase or melody and evaluating it to identify preferred options
using a listening diary/journal format to document ideas for compositions, interpretations, re-imaginings or performances
writing/notating a chart or lead-sheet to record ideas from a songwriting workshop or using software to write additional parts such as a bassline to accompany a melody

AC9AMU8D02.minimum_width: Reflect on at least one piece of music (own or others') using aural skills and music terminology; connect the reflection to at least one decision about their own composing or performing.
AC9AMU8D02.typical_width: Use aural skills and music terminology to identify and describe technical and expressive elements (chord progressions, phrasing, dynamics, articulation) in their own and others' music; use focused listening to evaluate recordings and inform interpretive decisions; use aural and visual cues when playing or singing in an ensemble.
wider: Compare two recordings of the same piece to evaluate how different interpretive choices realise stylistic features differently; justify which interpretation is more effective and why
Evaluate a recording of their own performance using the same criteria applied to others — identify at least one choice they would change and explain the musical reasoning
Analyse their own compositional or performance tendencies over time (e.g. always choosing the same dynamic range or rhythmic patterns) and deliberately experiment with alternatives
elaborations: practising, using aural skills and music terminology, how to identify and describe technical and expressive elements of music, such as chord progressions or the way a performer interprets, performs or shapes melodies, phrasing or dynamics; for example, when songwriting, in an instrumental music lesson or in a discussion with peers or a teacher

practising ways to use aural/visual cues when playing or singing in an ensemble; for example, chords or phrases that indicate place within a structure (aural) or gestures indicating tempo or entries (visual)
using focused listening and selected aural skills to evaluate the use of elements of music when listening to a recording for the purpose of making decisions about how they will interpret the music

AC9AMU8E01.minimum_width: Investigate how composers and/or performers use elements of music or compositional devices in music from at least one specified culture, time, place or context; describe at least two stylistic features using music terminology.
AC9AMU8E01.typical_width: Investigate how composers and/or performers use elements of music and compositional devices across multiple cultures, times, places or contexts; analyse performers' interpretations of composers' intentions using recordings and scores/charts; identify stylistic characteristics through listening; research social, cultural and historical developments relating to specific styles or traditions.
wider: Compare two recordings of the same work to evaluate where performers' interpretive choices diverge — assess which choices more effectively realise the composer's apparent intentions and justify the judgement

Investigate music composed to draw attention to social issues or values (protest songs, nationalistic music, music about identity or belonging) — analyse how specific musical choices serve the intended message

Research the social, cultural and historical developments that shaped a specific style or tradition (e.g. 32-bar song form, chamber music, singer-songwriter) and explain how these developments are reflected in the music's stylistic features
elaborations: accessing and researching music through live or recorded/streamed performances to analyse performers' interpretations of composers' intentions; for example, using recordings and score/s or chart/s or other information such as an interview or review to identify how performers have interpreted a composer's intentions, such as tempo choices, instrumentation, feel or articulation

listening to live or recorded music and identifying stylistic characteristics; for example, analysing how elements of music are manipulated and how compositional devices are used; then using this information to describe features of a style or to inform their performance of music in that style

listening to and evaluating how elements of music are manipulated in music composed by a range of composers, with the intention of drawing attention to social issues or values; for example, protest songs, nationalistic music, music that uses "folk"/traditional tunes in re-imagined ways, songs with lyrics that focus on themes such as identity or belonging

researching and discussing the influence of social, cultural and historical developments relating to specific styles, forms or traditions and incorporating these into their performance and/or compositions; for example, conventions relating to forms such as 32-bar song form, genres such as chamber music, or traditions such as singer-songwriter

AC9AMU8E02.minimum_width: Investigate the work of at least one First Nations Australian composer or performer; describe the styles or genres they draw on and explain at least one way ICIP rights are relevant to music practice.
AC9AMU8E02.typical_width: Investigate the diversity of music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians across different styles, genres and cultural contexts; explore how First Nations Australian composers and performers communicate ideas across communities and cultures; investigate when, how and why copyright and ICIP rights are relevant to practice as listeners, songwriters, composers and performers.
wider: Investigate the impacts of a First Nations Australian musician's work — consider what communities they reach, how their music has been received, and how they draw on multiple musical influences (traditional and contemporary)

Examine a case study illustrating protocols relating to ICIP rights in music — consider how the case clarifies when permission is required and what respectful, culturally responsive engagement looks like
Investigate issues relating to the use of First Nations Australian languages or stories in lyrics, songs or screen-based works — identify the ethical questions raised and the protocols that apply
elaborations: exploring ways that First Nations Australian composers and/or performers communicate their ideas and messages across communities and cultures; for example, by asking questions such as "What are the impacts of this musician's/these musicians' music?" and "What music styles or genres is this musician drawing on in creating their own music?"

investigating when, how and why copyright and/or Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights might be relevant to their practice as, for example, listeners, songwriters, composers and/or performers

exploring how protocols for protecting Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights exist to help students make ethical choices about how they use music, as listeners or creators; for example, by asking questions such as, "Who wrote this music?", "May I use ideas from this song, and do I need permission to do so?"

investigating issues relating to the use of First Nations Australian languages or stories in lyrics and songs or music for screen-based works; for example, considering case studies that illustrate protocols relating to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights

AC9AMU8P01.minimum_width: Perform music in at least one context (solo or ensemble) using appropriate posture and at least two relevant vocal/instrumental techniques; identify what worked and what would change in a future performance.
AC9AMU8P01.typical_width: Rehearse and perform a range of music in solo and ensemble contexts for a variety of audiences; apply correct posture and technical control; control tone and volume to create balanced ensemble sound; plan performances with expressive and stylistic goals; attend to how elements of music and vocal/instrumental techniques convey stylistic understanding.
wider: Analyse the performance practices of expert musicians in specific styles/genres — identify strategies for authentic stylistic interpretation and apply at least one strategy to rehearsal
Perform music across multiple styles or forms across a unit, demonstrating that technique and expressive choices are adapted to each style rather than applied uniformly
Plan and present an in-school performance that includes own composed or arranged music alongside other repertoire — evaluate how performing own work differs from performing existing repertoire
elaborations: rehearsing a range of music in solo and ensemble activities for performance to a variety of audiences

analysing the performance practices of musicians identified as experts in specific styles/genres to identify strategies for interpreting the styles authentically; for example, using online resources and creating a voice-over to add commentary to create a guide/set of aims for rehearsals

performing with correct posture, understanding that the body is part of the performance; for example, standing or sitting as appropriate for the instrument, ensemble, audience and any technology in use such as a microphone; maintaining technical control throughout the performance of a piece of music, controlling tone and volume to create a balanced sound in ensemble performance, reflecting and problem-solving to address imbalances in tone and volume in real-time and seeking feedback from the audience that they can use to reflect on and modify their musical practices in future performances

planning performances, rehearsing and performing their own vocal and/or instrumental compositions, individually or in a group, paying attention to expressive skills that convey stylistic understanding, such as articulation and accents
planning and presenting an in-school performance, attending to how they manipulate elements of music and use vocal/instrumental techniques to convey stylistic understanding
